findings.location: comparison_tables[0].rows[0]-rows[2]; decision_logic[1]; decision_logic[2]; quick_review[1]; quick_review[2]; quick_review[3]; exceptions[6]; timing_deadlines[2]; retrieval_prompts[4].answer; worked_examples[2].steps[2] and resolution; orientation[1]; orientation[4]; decision_logic[7]
findings.problem: The section teaches three 'different periods' belonging to three separate routes (2 days electronic where no exception applies; not more than 7 days written for a practitioner who 'has received' a s. 23(h) exception; not more than seven business days written or electronic for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under a 105 CMR 721.070(A) exception) and says 'the exam turns on keeping them apart', but the routes overlap and the section uses two incompatible tests for which one applies. (i) quick_review[1] limits the 7-day proviso to a practitioner who has 'RECEIVED' an exception, quick_review[3] and exceptions[6] say the categorical exceptions (outage, emergency, veterinarian, Schedule VI) are 'held by nobody', and decision_logic[1] sends any prescriber who 'has not received an electronic-prescribing exception from the commissioner' to the 2-day electronic default. On worked_examples[2]'s own facts (an oral Schedule IV prescription during an outage) decision_logic[1] therefore yields 2 days electronic while decision_logic[2] and the worked-example resolution yield seven business days. (ii) For emergencies the section reasons the other way: an enumerated 721.070(A) exception puts the prescription 'in the proviso by definition' (orientation[4], decision_logic[7]). Applied consistently, that places every 721.070(A)-exception oral prescription inside the s. 20(c) proviso, whose statutory text is 'not more than 7 days', which expires before seven business days; yet the section applies its 'shorter period controls' analysis only against federal law and never tells the candidate that the statute and the regulation state different periods for the same prescription. (iii) A practitioner holding a 105 CMR 721.075 time-limited waiver falls in both comparison_tables[0].rows[1] (7 days) and rows[2] (seven business days), and the section gives no rule for which governs.
findings.rationale: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) applies 'whenever a practitioner prescribes a controlled substance by oral prescription' (only Schedule VI is carved out) and states either 2 days (electronic) or, for a practitioner with a s. 23(h) exception, not more than 7 days (written). Section 23(h) makes the categorical exceptions (veterinarians, temporary technological or electrical failure, the time-limited waiver process, emergency situations, prescriptions issued outside the commonwealth and others) the commissioner's s. 23(h) exceptions, established 'through regulation'. 105 CMR 721.070(B) states seven business days for any oral Schedule II-V prescription under a 721.070(A) exception, and DCP Circular 19-12-108 repeats seven business days, so the regulatory figure is the Department's stated position; but no reading of s. 20(c) yields seven business days, and a regulation cannot lengthen a statutory period. As written, a candidate cannot extract one answer for an oral Schedule II-V prescription issued under a categorical exception or a waiver: the section's own entries give 2 days, 7 days or seven business days depending on which is read. The section needs one consistent test for the proviso and an explicit statement of how the regulation's seven business days relates to the statute's 7-day text (7 days being the count that satisfies both). The emergency Schedule II answer (7 days from the oral authorization) survives because the proviso and 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) coincide.

authorities.exact_section: DCP Circular 19-12-108 (12/27/2019), 'Written or Electronic Follow-Up Prescription' and 'Emergency Situations'

findings.location: orientation[3]; comparison_tables[1] (no row for what qualifies as an emergency); worked_examples[0].steps[0]; decision_logic[5]; role_duties[3]; ma_vs_federal[0]-[3]
findings.problem: The section says federal law 'reaches the same dispensing more narrowly' but identifies only the oral-only limb, the follow-up period, the face notation and the paper/electronic handling split. It never states the federal definition of emergency situation that 21 CFR 1306.11(d) incorporates from 21 CFR 290.10, which requires the prescribing practitioner to determine all three of: that immediate administration is necessary; that no appropriate alternative treatment is available, including administration of a drug that is not in Schedule II; and that it is not reasonably possible to provide a written prescription before the dispensing. The Massachusetts Emergency Situation in 105 CMR 721.010 is broader: it has no no-alternative-treatment element, it is met by either inability to generate or transmit an Electronic Prescription or a practitioner determination that the electronic requirement would cause a delay adversely affecting the patient, and it adds any other emergency defined in Department guidance. worked_examples[0] identifies the route solely by the Massachusetts definition, role_duties[3] has the practitioner check only 'the Emergency Situation elements', and decision_logic[5] applies the emergency route with no threshold test.
findings.rationale: On Massachusetts facts where the 721.010 definition is met but 290.10 is not (for example an appropriate non-Schedule II alternative is available, or only the 'delay' limb is met while a signed written prescription could be provided), 105 CMR 721.060(B) permits the oral Schedule II dispensing but 21 CFR 1306.11(d) does not, and 1306.11(a) then requires a written prescription signed by the practitioner. A section whose declared subject includes emergency dispensing, and which sets out an element-by-element Massachusetts-against-federal comparison of that dispensing, omits the federal condition that decides whether the oral route is open at all.

findings.problem: decision_logic[3] says that when a Schedule VI facsimile fails a 105 CMR 721.020(G) condition, including the additional-drug condition, 'the ordinary follow-up duty stands'. There is no follow-up duty for a Schedule VI oral prescription: s. 20(c) states that its requirements do not apply to Schedule VI, and 105 CMR 721.070(B) reaches only Schedules II through V. A disqualified facsimile is an Electronic Prescription transmitted through means other than Electronic Transmission, which 105 CMR 721.040(C) makes invalid; the Department's guidance states that for a Failover for gabapentin or another additional drug 'the pharmacist may not dispense the medication, and instead must contact the prescriber for a new written or oral prescription'. retrieval_prompts[6] likewise says a verified Failover 'excuses the written or electronic follow-up prescription that an oral prescription would otherwise owe', and quick_review[4] says 'Only such a document counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up'; every oral Schedule VI prescription needs no follow-up, as the section itself says at exceptions[0] and comparison_tables[0].rows[5].
findings.rationale: The legal work 721.020(G) does is validity: a verified Failover is treated as an oral prescription and may be dispensed, and a disqualified one is invalid and may not be. comparison_tables[2].rows[3] states this correctly, so the section contradicts itself, and a candidate following decision_logic[3] would dispense an additional drug on an invalid facsimile while waiting for a follow-up the law does not require.

findings.problem: The paraphrase of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) lists the pharmacist's written record as carrying the prescriber, the patient, the drug and strength, the directions and cautionary statements, the serial number and the refill information. Section 20(a) also requires the date of the prescription, the name of the dispensing pharmacy, the practitioner's address and registration number, the name of any expressly authorized representative, and the patient's address unless it is a veterinary prescription.
findings.rationale: The list is presented as the content of the duty, and the omitted date of the prescription is the start point for every date limit the guide teaches. Completing the list is a small edit.

authorities_checked.exact_section: 105 CMR 721.010 (Emergency Situation, Failover, Oral Prescription, Written Prescription), 721.020(A), (F), (G), 721.040(A), (C), 721.060(A)-(B)(5), 721.070(A)(1)-(12), (B), (C), 721.075 (Mass. Register #1531, 9/27/24)
DCP Circular 19-12-108 (12/27/2019): exceptions, follow-up, emergency situations, Failover

results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, severity Medium. I checked the emergency Schedule II material against the current texts and most of it is accurate: the Massachusetts written-or-orally-transmitted limb (105 CMR 721.060(B)); the federal oral-only exception (21 CFR 1306.11(a), (d)); the federal face requirement of both 'Authorization for Emergency Dispensing' and the date of the oral order; attaching a paper follow-up and annotating an electronic one; DEA notice and the voiding consequence; the central fill bar; the Schedule VI definition of Failover; and the no-verification rule in 721.070(C). Three Medium defects mean it cannot be published as it stands. (1) The follow-up 'routes' overlap. The section's own decision rules give 2 days, 7 days or seven business days on the facts of its worked example, and it never reconciles the statute's 2-day/7-day text with the regulation's seven business days. (2) The Massachusetts-versus-federal emergency comparison leaves out the 21 CFR 290.10 definition, which is narrower than 105 CMR 721.010: it requires that no appropriate alternative treatment be available. (3) It describes the consequence of Failover status wrongly. A disqualified Schedule VI facsimile is invalid and may not be dispensed; it does not revert to a follow-up duty. There is also one Low defect: the s. 20(a) element list is incomplete. MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0123 and MA-Q-0382 can all be answered from the section, and nothing in it contradicts them.

findings.location: exceptions[1]; quick_review[2]; retrieval_prompts[3].answer; exceptions[3]; orientation[0]; comparison_tables[0].rows[2].cells[2]
findings.problem: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d1/2) does not stop at the Maine-or-contiguous-state pathway. Its next paragraph provides that nothing in the subsection prohibits a retail pharmacy operating in the commonwealth from filling narcotic Schedule II prescriptions for residents of states other than Maine and the contiguous states, provided that: the pharmacy is licensed and registered as specified; the prescription is written by a practitioner (or an authorized nurse practitioner or physician assistant) licensed and registered in the same state as, or a state contiguous to, the state of delivery and registered under federal law; it is received by mail, commercial carrier or authorized electronic means; the pharmacist determines it is authentic, valid, legitimate and legal in the state from which it is received and verifies it; the pharmacy complies with the delivery state's reporting and prescription-monitoring requirements; and delivery is only by mail or commercial carrier to a verified address in the patient's state of residence. A further paragraph permits filling narcotic Schedule II prescriptions for patients admitted to long-term care facilities in Maine or a contiguous state, delivered directly by the pharmacy's courier. The section reduces all of this to 'Separate delivery provisions govern certain out-of-state residents' with none of the conditions, and elsewhere says flatly that the narcotic route 'reaches only a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth' (quick_review[2]) and that the subsections 'do not authorize mail order pharmacies' (exceptions[3]), without the retail mail-or-carrier delivery the same subsection allows.
findings.rationale: Take a Massachusetts retail pharmacy asked to fill a narcotic Schedule II prescription written by a Pennsylvania-registered physician for a Pennsylvania resident, and ship it by carrier to a verified Pennsylvania address. The section's statements answer 'no'; s. 18(d1/2) permits the fill on its stated conditions. The section names the framework without conveying its content, and the subsection it summarises contradicts its 'only' statements.

authorities.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d1/2), including the two unnumbered paragraphs that follow it (clauses (1)-(6) and (i)-(ii))

findings.problem: For s. 18(c) the section says the practitioner must be 'licensed and registered where they reside or practise'. Section 18(c) reads 'duly licensed and authorized to engage in prescriptive practice and duly registered in the state wherein he resides, if required, and duly registered under federal law to write prescriptions'. 'Resides or practices' is the wording of s. 18(d) and (d1/2), not (c). The section also omits the federal-registration condition, which s. 18(c) attaches to every prescription it reaches, Schedule VI included.
findings.rationale: The comparison table's 'Issuing-state condition' column exists to show how the three subsections differ. On this point it erases a textual difference and drops a condition.

findings.problem: In the table 'Duties that outlive the fill', the row 'Record having requested the practitioner's written prescription' carries 'Clock: 7 days, or the shorter federal period' and 'Measured from: The oral prescription'. That presents the seven days as a deadline on the pharmacist's recording duty, and presents the recording as a post-fill duty. Section 18(c) requires the pharmacist to 'record that he has requested that the practitioner deliver or mail to the dispensing pharmacy a written prescription ... within seven days or such shorter period required by Federal law'. The seven days is the period requested of the practitioner, and the record is made when the oral prescription is taken.
findings.rationale: timing_deadlines[4] and common_traps[3] in the same section state the allocation correctly ('The period governs the practitioner's delivery, not the pharmacist's recording'), so this row teaches the very trap the section warns against.

authorities.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), sentence on oral schedule III through V prescriptions

findings.location: orientation[3]; comparison_tables[1].rows[0]-rows[1]; worked_examples[2].steps[1] and steps[3]; retrieval_prompts[1]; retrieval_prompts[6].answer; ma_vs_federal[0]; common_traps[4]
findings.problem: The section calls the s. 18(c), (d) and (d1/2) windows 'presentation windows' and contrasts them with the s. 18(d3/4) five-day limit as 'measuring the dispensing rather than the presentation'. The statute gates the filling: each paragraph is valid only for 'authorizing the filling of prescriptions ... issued within the preceding' thirty or five days, so the operative date is the date of filling, not the date of presentation. 105 CMR 721.055(A), which implements the partial-fill limit, frames that limit as a presentation deadline: the prescription 'must be presented for initial partial fill not later than five calendar days after the Prescription issue date'. That is the reverse of the section's contrast.
findings.rationale: A candidate taught that the window governs presentation could accept a prescription presented inside the window and fill it after the window has closed. In substance both five-day rules require the first dispensing within five days of issue, with the remainder by day 30.

findings.problem: The section teaches the 30-day and 5-day windows and the 5-day partial-fill limit as running from 'the prescription issue date' but never states the counting convention. 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs the pharmacist to count the day after the prescription was written as day one, and 105 CMR 721.055(A) specifies five calendar days for the initial partial fill of a prescription from a prescriber outside the commonwealth.
findings.rationale: The start-point rule decides a five-day window at the margin, and the section's stated learning objective is to apply the correct window. The companion Schedule VI section teaches the rule; this section does not.

authorities_checked.exact_section: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a)-(d3/4), including the unnumbered paragraphs following (d1/2)
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 (definitions of 'Narcotic drug' and 'Practitioner')

results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, severity Medium. I checked the section against the current text of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18. These points are correct: the windows (30 days for schedules III-VI, 5 days for either Schedule II route); the authenticity-and-validity duty on all three pathways; telephone verification for schedules III-V and for both Schedule II routes, but not for Schedule VI; the rule against filling without verification and the liability protection for documented good-faith refusals; the Department copy within 30 days of filling, with the patient's name and address removed and outside the public-records law; and the s. 18(d3/4) partial-fill limits, same-pharmacy rule and patient-record notation. One Medium defect: the section teaches that the narcotic route reaches only Maine and contiguous-state practitioners, but the later paragraphs of s. 18(d1/2) let a Massachusetts retail pharmacy fill and ship narcotic Schedule II prescriptions for residents of other states, and for long-term-care patients in Maine or a contiguous state. The section mentions 'separate delivery provisions' without saying what they allow. Four Low defects: (1) the s. 18(c) issuing condition is misstated ('resides or practises', and federal registration is omitted); (2) a table row attaches the 7-day period to the pharmacist's recording duty, which contradicts the section's own timing entries; (3) the 'presentation window' label is wrong, because the statute gates the filling; (4) no day-counting convention is given for the windows. MA-Q-0027, MA-Q-0034, MA-Q-0124 and MA-Q-0424 can all be answered from the section, and nothing in it contradicts them.

findings.problem: The section states that for a reportable dispensing, including a Schedule VI additional drug, the data go to the Department 'by the end of the next business day'. That is 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5). M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires each pharmacy to submit the information in accordance with the Department's transmission methods and frequency requirements, 'provided, however, that the information shall be submitted at least once every 24 hours'. The section never mentions the statutory limit.
findings.rationale: The statute is a shorter limit that reaches the same dispensing. For an additional drug dispensed on a Friday, the section's answer (end of Monday) would leave more than 24 hours without a submission, which s. 24A(c) does not permit; the same is true across any holiday. A deadline taught from the regulation alone gives the wrong answer on those facts.

findings.problem: The paragraph introduces two date gates, the one-year validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12) and the thirty-day out-of-state window in s. 18(c), then says 'When the applicable clock has run, the only thing left is the narrow professional-judgment continuation'. The 14-day continuation in 247 CMR 9.04(12) attaches to a Schedule VI prescription that 'expires or has no remaining refills'. Nothing extends it to an out-of-state prescription after the statutory authority lapses, and s. 18(c) is 'valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions, issued within the preceding thirty days'.
findings.rationale: The sentence invites a candidate to dispense a bridge supply on a 45-day-old out-of-state Schedule VI prescription. The section's own worked_examples[1] correctly concludes that such a prescription may not be filled and does not offer the continuation, so the orientation sentence is also inconsistent with it.

findings.problem: Both present 'a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled' (105 CMR 721.020(D)(6)) as content 'beyond the statutory element list'. But M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) itself requires 'a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled', as the section's own forms_records[3] correctly says; the Schedule II opioid partial-fill notation, while outside s. 22(a), is also statutory under s. 22(c). forms_records[4] also says 721.020(D)(4) 'leaves the patient name and address blank' on naloxone and 721.070(A)(7) or (A)(12) prescriptions, where the regulation says they 'may be left blank'. It also cites (A)(7) and (A)(12) without saying they cover expedited partner therapy for chlamydia, and prescriptions for a public health emergency, sexually transmitted infections or other urgent public health matters.
findings.rationale: The retrieval prompt tests exactly this statute-versus-regulation attribution, and its answer key is wrong on one of its three items, contradicting forms_records[3]. The underlying prescription-content duty is unaffected.

findings.problem: exceptions[2] says that because 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 9.04(14), 'the customer-identifier duty' falls away for that facility type, and orientation[1] assigns the customer identifier to the Board's 247 CMR. 9.04(15) removes only the Board's 9.04(14) requirement. 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3) independently requires a pharmacy subject to the monitoring-program reporting requirement to require a customer identifier whenever a Schedule II-V substance or an additional drug is dispensed; 700.012(A)(2) excludes only medication-order dispensing to hospital inpatients. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c)(2) directs that requirement.
findings.rationale: A second source that the Board's exclusion does not reach imposes the same duty, so the absolute statement overstates what the exclusion does.

findings.problem: The paragraph says the two one-year rules 'sit in two different chapters'. 247 CMR 9.04(12) and 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) are two sections of the same chapter, 247 CMR 9.00.
findings.rationale: The substantive point, that two rules answer two different questions, is right; the description of where they sit is not.

DCP Circular 19-12-108 (12/27/2019): Schedule VI exception, follow-up, Failover

results.summary: MINOR_EDIT, severity Medium. These points check out against current text: the Schedule VI definition (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(6); 105 CMR 700.002(F), which ties Schedules I-V to 21 CFR 1308.11-1308.15); the 721.070(A)(9) exception; the written-format rules in 721.020(F) and invalidity under 721.040(A); the Schedule VI carve-out from s. 20(c); the Failover definition and its additional-drug disqualifier; 247 CMR 9.04(10), (12) with the 14-day continuation, (14) and (15); 247 CMR 9.14(1)-(4)(c), covering the timely-transfer duty, acting as the patient's agent, no transfer fee, the III-V manner, remaining refills and the one-year transfer bar; 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) ('Schedule VI only', with pharmacist approval); the additional-drug designation and notice in 700.012(C)(8); and 721.020(D)-(E). One Medium defect: the prescription-monitoring transmission deadline is taught only as 'by the end of the next business day' (105 CMR 700.012(A)(5)), although M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires submission at least once every 24 hours. Four Low defects: (1) the 14-day continuation is implicitly extended to the out-of-state 30-day gate; (2) the refill statement is wrongly described as beyond the statutory element list; (3) the customer-identifier duty is said to fall away for institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, although 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3) imposes it independently; (4) two sections of 247 CMR 9.00 are described as 'two different chapters'. MA-Q-0116, MA-Q-0118 and MA-Q-0120 can all be answered from the section, and nothing in it contradicts them.
